Deep Dive: Anthropic S-1 Myths and Mythos — Jamin Ball, Altimeter102 min49 insights2026-11-07
▶ Watch on YouTube
Altimeter's Jamin Ball walks through Anthropic's S-1, arguing it reveals a 'almost accidentally profitable' frontier lab (85% gross margin, 21% FCF margin, ~$7B lifetime burn against $16.8B quarterly revenue) driven by a ~7x inference-efficiency gain, and that the $108B convert liability and ~$81B H1 net loss are accounting artifacts of valuation appreciation. He frames the investment case as whether Anthropic can stay at the frontier, with a large untapped enterprise token-spend TAM, while flagging debt-market indigestion and multi-trillion-dollar infrastructure buildout constraints.

Mini Brains, Beating Heart Organoids, and the AI That Predicts Them — Fabian Theis, Helmholtz Munich51 min36 insights2026-11-06
▶ Watch on YouTube
Fabian Theis (Helmholtz Munich) argues virtual-cell / perturbation-prediction models are finally taking off because perturbation-space data is exploding (organoids, CRISPR screens, 1,000-drug batteries), but warns that linear baselines still win on simple tasks and that the real commercial moat is proprietary data generation plus lab-in-the-loop experiment steering (his new 'Lab Compass' inverse generative model), not platform models alone. He also outlines why Germany/Europe creates startups at US-like rates but fails at Series A/B scaling.

Virtual cell revival driven by perturbation data 7
Biohub announced a $1.8 billion collaboration with the DOE, NIH, Meta and Google to collect and open-source multiscale biological data for a new generation of virtual cell models, coupled to the Human Cell Atlas consortium.
data_point🗣 RJ Honicky (host) / Fabian Theisconviction: highBiohubDOENIHMetaGoogleHuman Cell Atlas
So what: Big-tech and government money is flowing into cell-level biological data, a counterweight to the molecule-design focus of Anthropic/OpenAI biopharma initiatives.
“Biohub just announced a $1.8 billion collaboration with the DOE, NIH, Meta, and Google to collect and open-source multiscale biological data that can be used to develop a new generation of virtual cells.” ▶ 2:32
Theis believes generative and lab-in-the-loop methods that worked at the molecule level are now being exported one level up to the cell level, and that perturbation-prediction 'virtual cell' startups are exploding across the US, Europe and China.

So what: Expect a wave of cell-level AI-bio startups, not just structural/molecule design companies.

The genuine demand driver for virtual cell models is that pharma desperately needs cell-type context-specific screens, which it cannot yet do; Theis hopes the boom is not just companies bolting AI onto products.

“pharma is really desperately uh needing to be cell type context-specific in their screens, which at the moment they can't do yet.” ▶ 5:42
Early perturbation models (Theis lab's scGen, 2019) were near-linear shifts in latent space and only did 'okay' because datasets and questions were simplistic; the perturbation space (control vs disease) was far scarcer than the cell observation space.
causal🗣 Fabian Theisconviction: highscGenHelmholtz Munich
So what: The bottleneck for virtual cells has been perturbation diversity, not cell counts.
Perturbation data is now exploding in scale: single experiments measuring 10 million transcriptomes, ~100 cell lines with full CRISPR Perturb-seq, or batteries of 1,000 drugs, which makes rich perturbation prediction possible.
data_point🗣 Fabian Theisconviction: highPac BioPerturb-seqCRISPR

Bitter lesson vs inductive bias and scaling 5
Theis says literature has shown over decades that building strong a priori inductive biases into models costs predictive power, but because perturbation-space data is still not in a super data-rich regime, hybrid models remain the right choice in biology for now.
thesis🗣 Fabian Theisconviction: mediumbitter lesson
So what: Near-term winners in bio-AI may combine priors with data; pure scale plays need more perturbation data first.
“I don't think we're yet in the super data rich regime. So, I think in our case these hybrid models might be still the thing to go for” ▶ 19:04
Theis predicts that in the long run the most-used biology models will be flexible, data-driven ones with interpretation added a posteriori, citing AlphaFold, where later versions learned rotation symmetry from data rather than having it built in.
prediction🗣 Fabian Theisconviction: mediumAlphaFold
So what: Data scale ultimately beats hand-engineered biology priors, favoring whoever owns the biggest datasets.
“at some point data beats human-made additional concepts in these models.” ▶ 19:18
Early single-cell foundation model papers failed to demonstrate scaling laws, producing an overhyped phase followed by a sobering-up; reviewers now demand proper scaling-law evidence before buying in.
contrarian🗣 Fabian Theisconviction: highfoundation models

“people haven't really shown that you need this complexity to actually sort of really scale up.” ▶ 23:09
Theis lab's contrastive model scConcept (SE concept) shows strong scaling: the paper compared against Geneformer at ~30 million cells, and a Hugging Face release uses 350 million cells across 16 species with up to ~100 million parameters, with nice scaling behavior starting to emerge.
data_point🗣 Fabian Theisconviction: highSE conceptGene FormerHugging Face
So what: Single-cell models are beginning to show scaling behavior at hundreds of millions of cells, approaching a data-driven regime.
“on on Hugging Face now, we have a 350 million cell model with I think going up to maybe 100 million parameters” ▶ 23:42
Self-supervised learning for single-cell data is still unsettled: approaches copy NLP masked autoencoders, tabular foundation models, JEPA-style and contrastive methods, with losses and representations still debated.

Virtual cells as world models and baselines 7
Theis frames a perturbation-prediction virtual cell as a world model f(x, a) that predicts next state x' from state x and action a; representation learning learns the state space, but a separate generative model (e.g. flow matching) is needed to push forward along the action.
framework🗣 Fabian Theisconviction: highworld modelflow matching
So what: Pure foundation-model embeddings are not enough for perturbation prediction; generative dynamics layers are required.
“it's not just a model that is sort of f of x, but f of x {comma} a, right?” ▶ 24:47
Theis lab's CellFlow paper (accepted at Nature Methods) shows flow-matching approaches are much better at generating perturbation effects, but depend heavily on a good latent space.
data_point🗣 Fabian Theisconviction: highcell flowNature Methodsflow matching
So what: Flow matching on strong latent spaces is emerging as the leading perturbation-prediction recipe.
For cell type prediction within an organ, near state-of-the-art models are still logistic regression (Theis's paper was titled 'Deep learning is not needed for cell type prediction'), whereas cross-organ prediction benefits from nonlinear models like scTab.

Quantedge CEO Suhaimi Zainul Abidin explains how the ~$8B Singapore systematic fund harvests risk premia across ~300 markets plus insurance-linked securities, deliberately targeting ~25% volatility instead of the institutional 8-12% norm. He argues low volatility leaves return on the table, that total risk (vol, tails, correlation, margin, liquidity) and lockups/perpetual share classes are what make a levered strategy survivable, and cites a 29% March 2020 loss as the defining stress test.

Quantedge defines a risk premia strategy as accepting risk in exchange for expected return, analogous to an insurer charging above fair value for risk others want to offload.

So what: Frames every market as a place to be paid for warehousing risk others want to shed.
“A risk premia strategy is one which accepts risk essentially in exchange for uh an expected return.” ▶ 9:15
Suhaimi argues most markets exist for the purpose of risk transfer, and that taking that risk (equity, bond, commodity) deserves a return the market adjusts to provide.
thesis🗣 Suhaimi Zainul Abidin (CEO, Quantedge)conviction: highrisk premia
So what: Underpins a strategy of harvesting premia across all asset classes rather than forecasting.
“In fact, we think most markets exist for the purpose of risk transfer” ▶ 10:13
Quantedge describes itself not as a trend follower/CTA but as systematic global macro whose core is market risk premia layered with long-short factor-based market-neutral strategies, essentially a capital-efficiency vehicle.
framework🗣 Suhaimi Zainul Abidin (CEO, Quantedge)conviction: highQuantedgeCTA

framework🗣 Suhaimi Zainul Abidin (CEO, Quantedge)conviction: highrisk premia

Quantedge invests in insurance-linked securities (cat bonds etc.), where it expects potentially around 20% returns over cash in some years and over the long term.

Abstract Ventures' Ram describes a 2021-like but better-founded AI venture market: 3-5x secondary 'tranches', 4x valuation dispersion, mega-funds deploying 3x faster than planned and delaying funding, LP liquidity concentrated in SpaceX/Anthropic/OpenAI/Databricks, and neo-lab compute demand hinging on debt markets. He argues alpha lies in proactive bets on great founders in non-obvious markets (e.g., Conduit BCI) and rates froth 6.5-7/10 versus opportunity 10/10.

Deal-level froth and tranche pricing 9
In the current venture market, investors who lose a hot primary round now buy into a simultaneous secondary tranche at roughly 3-5x the primary price, versus the 2021 'fast follow' at about 2x a couple of weeks later.
data_point🗣 Ram (Abstract Ventures)conviction: highventure capital
So what: Same-round price dispersion of 3-5x means entry price depends heavily on which tranche an investor gets.

“So I don't think that tranching is like a thing that's an unhealthy sign of the market.” ▶ 2:26
Valuation dispersion for a single deal has become so erratic that an experienced investor's estimate of clearing price can span about a 4x range, because one bidder may pay triple the second-highest bid to avoid losing the deal.
data_point🗣 Ram (Abstract Ventures)conviction: highventure capital
So what: Price discovery in private markets is breaking down; comps are anchored on outlier prints.

Did the Midterms Destroy All Hope for Data Centers? | E236067 min39 insights2026-11-06

After Democrats took both the House and Senate in the 2026 midterms on a platform that partly targeted AI data center construction, Jason Calacanis argues that the anti-data-center stance is campaign posturing. He expects a negotiated 'good neighbor' compromise (pay for power, protect water, pay taxes), calls the 5-6% tech selloff a generational buying opportunity, and covers AI copyright licensing (Anthropic-AP), Apple's AI spending caps, rising enterprise AI seat prices, and coming wealth and asset taxes.

Vik Uppal of Maverick argues that six years of CRE stress with elevated rates and regional-bank retreat have created one of the best restructuring/recapitalization opportunity sets he has seen, best captured by a flexible, capital-preservation-first mandate targeting 'tweener' and middle-market deals that large platforms miss. Lawfare Daily: The President’s Hand in Russia’s Covert Action46 min32 insights2026-11-06

Former CIA officer Julia Curley (with Benjamin Wittes) applies Langley's covert-action metrics to Russia's 2016 election operation. She argues it met all three ICA goals and that Russia's biggest dividends came afterward from Trump himself, who denied the interference and dismantled the defenses while Russia's AI-deepfake interference continues into the 2026 midterms. She proposes statutory protections and mandatory public assessments to counter the beneficiary's 'winner's veto'.
